claim: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a common and progressive spinal deformity in children.
source: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a common and progressive spinal deformity in children that exhibits striking sexual dimorphism, with girls at more than fivefold greater risk of severe disease compared to boys.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about AIS that is part of established medical knowledge.

claim: Girls have more than fivefold greater risk of severe AIS compared to boys.
source: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a common and progressive spinal deformity in children that exhibits striking sexual dimorphism, with girls at more than fivefold greater risk of severe disease compared to boys.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Karol et al., 1993 in the Introduction section.

claim: A female-specific AIS genetic risk locus exists in an enhancer near the PAX1 gene.
source: We previously defined a female-specific AIS genetic risk locus in an enhancer near the PAX1 gene.
evidence: This refers to prior work by the authors as indicated by 'We previously defined'.

claim: A variant in COL11A1 (rs3753841; NM_080629.2_c.4004C>T; p.(Pro1335Leu)) is significantly associated with AIS with p=7.07E-11 and OR=1.118.
source: In a genetic study of 10,519 individuals with AIS and 93,238 unaffected controls, significant association was identified with a variant in COL11A1 encoding collagen (α1) XI (rs3753841; NM_080629.2_c.4004C>T; p.(Pro1335Leu); p=7.07E–11, OR = 1.118).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the genetic association study presented in the manuscript with statistical evidence.

claim: PAX1 protein localizes within the intervertebral disc-vertebral junction region in postnatal spines.
source: In postnatal spines we found that PAX1 and collagen (α1) XI protein both localize within the intervertebral disc-vertebral junction region encompassing the growth plate, with less collagen (α1) XI detected in Pax1-/- spines compared to wild-type.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Collagen (α1) XI protein localizes within the intervertebral disc-vertebral junction region in postnatal spines.
source: In postnatal spines we found that PAX1 and collagen (α1) XI protein both localize within the intervertebral disc-vertebral junction region encompassing the growth plate, with less collagen (α1) XI detected in Pax1-/- spines compared to wild-type.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Less collagen (α1) XI is detected in Pax1-/- spines compared to wild-type.
source: In postnatal spines we found that PAX1 and collagen (α1) XI protein both localize within the intervertebral disc-vertebral junction region encompassing the growth plate, with less collagen (α1) XI detected in Pax1-/- spines compared to wild-type.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Wild-type Col11a1 expression in costal chondrocytes suppresses expression of Pax1.
source: By genetic targeting we found that wild-type Col11a1 expression in costal chondrocytes suppresses expression of Pax1 and of Mmp3, encoding the matrix metalloproteinase 3 enzyme implicated in matrix remodeling.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Wild-type Col11a1 expression in costal chondrocytes suppresses expression of Mmp3.
source: By genetic targeting we found that wild-type Col11a1 expression in costal chondrocytes suppresses expression of Pax1 and of Mmp3, encoding the matrix metalloproteinase 3 enzyme implicated in matrix remodeling.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The AIS-associated COL11A1P1335L mutant abrogates suppression of Mmp3.
source: However, the latter suppression was abrogated in the presence of the AIS-associated COL11A1P1335L mutant.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Knockdown of the estrogen receptor gene Esr2 significantly alters Col11a1 expression in chondrocytes.
source: Further, we found that either knockdown of the estrogen receptor gene Esr2 or tamoxifen treatment significantly altered Col11a1 and Mmp3 expression in chondrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Tamoxifen treatment significantly alters Col11a1 expression in chondrocytes.
source: Further, we found that either knockdown of the estrogen receptor gene Esr2 or tamoxifen treatment significantly altered Col11a1 and Mmp3 expression in chondrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockdown of Esr2 significantly alters Mmp3 expression in chondrocytes.
source: Further, we found that either knockdown of the estrogen receptor gene Esr2 or tamoxifen treatment significantly altered Col11a1 and Mmp3 expression in chondrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Tamoxifen treatment significantly alters Mmp3 expression in chondrocytes.
source: Further, we found that either knockdown of the estrogen receptor gene Esr2 or tamoxifen treatment significantly altered Col11a1 and Mmp3 expression in chondrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Genetic variation and estrogen signaling increase AIS susceptibility by altering a PAX1-COL11a1-MMP3 signaling axis in spinal chondrocytes.
source: We propose a new molecular model of AIS pathogenesis wherein genetic variation and estrogen signaling increase disease susceptibility by altering a PAX1-COL11a1-MMP3 signaling axis in spinal chondrocytes.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the integration of multiple experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: AIS is reported in all major ancestral groups with a population prevalence of 1.5–3%.
source: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is reported in all major ancestral groups, with a population prevalence of 1.5–3% (Wise, 2014; Hresko, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Wise, 2014 and Hresko, 2013.

claim: Children with AIS usually present with a characteristic right-thoracic major curve pattern and a compensatory lumbar curve.
source: Children with AIS usually present with a characteristic right-thoracic major curve pattern and a compensatory lumbar curve.
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by citation to Richards et al., 2020.

claim: Major thoracolumbar and lumbar curves are less frequent in AIS.
source: Major thoracolumbar and lumbar curves are less frequent (Richards et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Richards et al., 2020.

claim: The three-dimensional nature of AIS deformity results in torsion in the spine that is most significant at the apex of the major curve.
source: The three-dimensional nature of the deformity results in torsion in the spine that is most significant at the apex of the major curve, and changes in the structures of the vertebrae and ribs may develop as the curve worsens or progresses (Richards et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Richards et al., 2020.

claim: Changes in the structures of the vertebrae and ribs may develop as the AIS curve worsens or progresses.
source: The three-dimensional nature of the deformity results in torsion in the spine that is most significant at the apex of the major curve, and changes in the structures of the vertebrae and ribs may develop as the curve worsens or progresses (Richards et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Richards et al., 2020.

claim: Children with thoracic curves are at increased risk of AIS progression.
source: Children with thoracic curves, with larger curves at first presentation, and/or with greater remaining growth potential are at increased risk of progression, but this risk decreases sharply after skeletal maturity (Richards et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Richards et al., 2020.

claim: Children with larger curves at first presentation are at increased risk of AIS progression.
source: Children with thoracic curves, with larger curves at first presentation, and/or with greater remaining growth potential are at increased risk of progression, but this risk decreases sharply after skeletal maturity (Richards et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Richards et al., 2020.

claim: Children with greater remaining growth potential are at increased risk of AIS progression.
source: Children with thoracic curves, with larger curves at first presentation, and/or with greater remaining growth potential are at increased risk of progression, but this risk decreases sharply after skeletal maturity (Richards et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Richards et al., 2020.

claim: The risk of AIS progression decreases sharply after skeletal maturity.
source: Children with thoracic curves, with larger curves at first presentation, and/or with greater remaining growth potential are at increased risk of progression, but this risk decreases sharply after skeletal maturity (Richards et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Richards et al., 2020.

claim: Girls have at least a fivefold greater risk of progressive AIS deformity requiring treatment compared to boys.
source: Sex is a recognized risk factor for AIS, with girls having at least a fivefold greater risk of progressive deformity requiring treatment compared to boys (Karol et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Karol et al., 1993.

claim: Levels of circulating endocrine hormones, particularly estrogen, are speculated to be important exposures in AIS susceptibility.
source: This well-documented sexual dimorphism has prompted speculation that levels of circulating endocrine hormones, particularly estrogen, are important exposures in AIS susceptibility (Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation to Liang et al., 2021.

claim: The genetic architecture of human AIS is complex.
source: The genetic architecture of human AIS is complex, and underlying disease mechanisms remain uncertain.
evidence: This is a general statement about AIS genetics supported by the literature.

claim: Underlying disease mechanisms of AIS remain uncertain.
source: The genetic architecture of human AIS is complex, and underlying disease mechanisms remain uncertain.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Heritability studies suggest that AIS disease risk is multifactorial, caused by genetic and environmental contributions.
source: Heritability studies of Northern European (Wynne-Davies, 1968; Grauers et al., 2012), North American (Riseborough and Wynne-Davies, 1973; Kruse et al., 2012), and South Asian (Tang et al., 2012) ancestral groups suggest that disease risk is multifactorial, caused by genetic and environmental contributions (Wise, 2014; Wise et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to heritability studies.

claim: Population-based GWAS in multiple ancestral groups have identified several AIS-associated susceptibility loci, mostly within non-coding genomic regions.
source: Accordingly, population-based genome-wide association studies (GWAS) in multiple ancestral groups have identified several AIS-associated susceptibility loci, mostly within non-coding genomic regions (Wise et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wise et al., 2020.

claim: Multiple GWAS have implicated non-coding regions near the LBX1 gene in AIS.
source: In particular, multiple GWAS have implicated non-coding regions near the LBX1 (Takahashi et al., 2011), ADGRG6 (also known as GRP126) (Kou et al., 2013), and BNC2 (Ogura et al., 2015) genes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Takahashi et al., 2011.

claim: Multiple GWAS have implicated non-coding regions near the ADGRG6 gene in AIS.
source: In particular, multiple GWAS have implicated non-coding regions near the LBX1 (Takahashi et al., 2011), ADGRG6 (also known as GRP126) (Kou et al., 2013), and BNC2 (Ogura et al., 2015) genes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kou et al., 2013.

claim: Multiple GWAS have implicated non-coding regions near the BNC2 gene in AIS.
source: In particular, multiple GWAS have implicated non-coding regions near the LBX1 (Takahashi et al., 2011), ADGRG6 (also known as GRP126) (Kou et al., 2013), and BNC2 (Ogura et al., 2015) genes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ogura et al., 2015.

claim: Association with alleles in an enhancer distal to PAX1 was primarily driven by females.
source: An association with alleles in an enhancer distal to PAX1, encoding the transcription factor paired box 1, was primarily driven by females, suggesting that it contributes to the sexual dimorphism observed in AIS (Sharma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sharma et al., 2015.

claim: Meta-analysis of combined AIS GWAS identified variants in an intron of SOX6 as AIS susceptibility loci.
source: Subsequent meta-analysis of combined AIS GWAS identified additional susceptibility loci. These included variants in an intron of SOX6, a transcription factor, that along with PAX1, is important in early spinal column formation (Smits and Lefebvre, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smits and Lefebvre, 2003.

claim: SOX6 is important in early spinal column formation.
source: Subsequent meta-analysis of combined AIS GWAS identified additional susceptibility loci. These included variants in an intron of SOX6, a transcription factor, that along with PAX1, is important in early spinal column formation (Smits and Lefebvre, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smits and Lefebvre, 2003.

claim: PAX1 is important in early spinal column formation.
source: Subsequent meta-analysis of combined AIS GWAS identified additional susceptibility loci. These included variants in an intron of SOX6, a transcription factor, that along with PAX1, is important in early spinal column formation (Smits and Lefebvre, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smits and Lefebvre, 2003.

claim: Gene enrichment analyses found significant correlation of AIS-associated loci with biological pathways involving cartilage and connective tissue development.
source: Furthermore, gene enrichment analyses found significant correlation of AIS-associated loci with biological pathways involving cartilage and connective tissue development (Khanshour et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Khanshour et al., 2018.

claim: A GWAS in a Japanese population identified 14 additional AIS loci.
source: A more recent GWAS in a Japanese population identified 14 additional AIS loci that are candidates for further evaluation (Kou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kou et al., 2019.

claim: Genome sequencing in AIS cases and families identified enrichment of rare variants in the COL11A2 gene.
source: In separate studies, genome sequencing in AIS cases and families identified enrichment of rare variants in the COL11A2 (Haller et al., 2016) and HSPG2 (Baschal et al., 2014) genes, encoding components of the cartilage extracellular matrix (ECM).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haller et al., 2016.

claim: Genome sequencing in AIS cases and families identified enrichment of rare variants in the HSPG2 gene.
source: In separate studies, genome sequencing in AIS cases and families identified enrichment of rare variants in the COL11A2 (Haller et al., 2016) and HSPG2 (Baschal et al., 2014) genes, encoding components of the cartilage extracellular matrix (ECM).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baschal et al., 2014.

claim: COL11A2 encodes a component of the cartilage extracellular matrix.
source: In separate studies, genome sequencing in AIS cases and families identified enrichment of rare variants in the COL11A2 (Haller et al., 2016) and HSPG2 (Baschal et al., 2014) genes, encoding components of the cartilage extracellular matrix (ECM).
evidence: This is established knowledge about COL11A2 function.

claim: HSPG2 encodes a component of the cartilage extracellular matrix.
source: In separate studies, genome sequencing in AIS cases and families identified enrichment of rare variants in the COL11A2 (Haller et al., 2016) and HSPG2 (Baschal et al., 2014) genes, encoding components of the cartilage extracellular matrix (ECM).
evidence: This is established knowledge about HSPG2 function.

claim: Variation affecting cartilage and connective tissue ECM is an emerging theme in the heterogeneous genetic architecture of AIS.
source: Hence, variation affecting cartilage and connective tissue ECM is an emerging theme in the heterogeneous genetic architecture of AIS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the accumulation of genetic findings cited in the manuscript.

claim: Several genetic mutants in zebrafish with larval or later-onset spinal deformity have been described, including ptk7.
source: In zebrafish, several genetic mutants with larval or later-onset spinal deformity have been described, including ptk7 (Hayes et al., 2014; Van Gennip et al., 2018), c21orf59 (Jaffe et al., 2016), ccdc40 (Becker-Heck et al., 2011), ccdc151 (Bachmann-Gagescu et al., 2011), dyx1c1, and kif6 (Konjikusic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hayes et al., 2014 and Van Gennip et al., 2018.

claim: Missense variants in COL11A2 associated with human congenital scoliosis fail to rescue a vertebral malformation phenotype in a zebrafish col11a2 knockout line.
source: In rescue experiments, Rebello et al. recently showed that missense variants in COL11A2 associated with human congenital scoliosis fail to rescue a vertebral malformation phenotype in a zebrafish col11a2 knockout line (Rebello et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rebello et al., 2023.

claim: Conditional deletion of Adgrg6 in skeletal cartilage produces a progressive scoliosis of the thoracic spine during postnatal development in mice.
source: In mouse, conditional deletion of Adgrg6 in skeletal cartilage (using Col2a1-Cre) produces a progressive scoliosis of the thoracic spine during postnatal development that is marked by herniations within the cartilaginous endplates of involved vertebrae.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Long et al., 2001; Liu et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021.

claim: Progressive scoliosis was observed when Adgrg6 was deleted from committed chondrocytes in mice.
source: Progressive scoliosis, albeit to a lesser extent, was also observed when Adgrg6 was deleted from committed chondrocytes (using ATC:Cre) (Long et al., 2001; Liu et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Long et al., 2001; Liu et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021.

claim: Cartilage and possibly other osteochondroprogenitor cells contribute to the scoliosis phenotype in Adgrg6 deletion mouse models.
source: These studies demonstrate that cartilage and possibly other osteochondroprogenitor cells contribute to the scoliosis phenotype in these models (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: Deficiencies in biogenesis and/or homeostasis of cartilage, intervertebral disc, and dense connective tissues undermine the maintenance of proper spinal alignment during the adolescent growth spurt.
source: Taken together, genetic and functional studies in mouse, although limited, support the hypothesis that deficiencies in biogenesis and/or homeostasis of cartilage, intervertebral disc (IVD), and dense connective tissues undermine the maintenance of proper spinal alignment during the adolescent growth spurt (Wise et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to Wise et al., 2020 and inference from the cited studies.

claim: The combined contribution of reported AIS-associated variants is broadly estimated to account for less than 10% of the overall genetic risk of the disease.
source: The combined contribution of reported AIS-associated variants is broadly estimated to account for less than 10% of the overall genetic risk of the disease (Kou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kou et al., 2019.

claim: Two nonsynonymous variants, in COL11A1 (rs3753841) and MMP14 (rs1042704), were significantly associated with AIS in the discovery cohort.
source: Two nonsynonymous variants, in COL11A1 (rs3753841; NM_080629.2_c.4004C>T; p.(Pro1335Leu); odds ratio (OR)=1.236 [95% CI = 1.134–1.347], p=1.17E–06) and MMP14 (rs1042704; NM_004995.4_c.817G>A; p.(Asp273Asn); OR = 1.239 [95% CI = 1.125–1.363], p=1.89E–05) were significantly associated with AIS (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the discovery study with statistical evidence shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The association with rs3753841 in COL11A1 remained statistically significant in females.
source: In females, the association with rs3753841 remained statistically significant, whereas rs1042704, near MMP14, was not associated with AIS in females (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sex-stratified analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: rs1042704 near MMP14 was not associated with AIS in females.
source: In females, the association with rs3753841 remained statistically significant, whereas rs1042704, near MMP14, was not associated with AIS in females (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sex-stratified analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Meta-analysis of all cohorts together increased the evidence for association of both rs3753841 and rs1042704 variants with AIS risk.
source: Meta-analysis of all cohorts together increased the evidence for association of both variants with AIS risk (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by meta-analysis results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Rare dominant mutations in COL11A1 can cause Marshall syndrome (MRSHS).
source: Rare dominant mutations in COL11A1, often disrupting a Gly-X-Y sequence, can cause Marshall (MRSHS) (OMIM #154780) or Stickler syndromes (STL2) (OMIM #604841) marked variously by facial anomalies, sensineural hearing loss, short stature, spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, eye anomalies, ectodermal features, and scoliosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about COL11A1 mutations and their clinical consequences.

claim: Rare dominant mutations in COL11A1 can cause Stickler syndrome (STL2).
source: Rare dominant mutations in COL11A1, often disrupting a Gly-X-Y sequence, can cause Marshall (MRSHS) (OMIM #154780) or Stickler syndromes (STL2) (OMIM #604841) marked variously by facial anomalies, sensineural hearing loss, short stature, spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, eye anomalies, ectodermal features, and scoliosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about COL11A1 mutations and their clinical consequences.

claim: The AIS cohort and individuals carrying the rs3753841 risk allele were negative for co-morbidities or obvious features of Marshall or Stickler syndromes.
source: Notably, our AIS cohort and particularly individuals carrying the rs3753841 risk allele were negative for co-morbidities or obvious features of Marshall or Stickler syndromes.
evidence: This is an observation from the study cohort.

claim: Variation in COL11A1 is independently associated with AIS.
source: Thus, variation in COL11A1 is independently associated with AIS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic association data and the absence of syndromic features in the cohort.

claim: COL11A1 was upregulated in cartilage relative to bone and muscle in adolescent human spinal tissues.
source: We analyzed RNAseq datasets derived from adolescent human spinal tissues (Makki et al., 2020), finding that COL11A1 was upregulated in cartilage relative to bone and muscle.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: PAX1 and COL11A2 showed the strongest expression levels relative to other published human AIS-associated genes in cartilage.
source: In cartilage, PAX1 and COL11A2 showed the strongest expression levels relative to other published human AIS-associated genes (Kou et al., 2013; Ogura et al., 2015; Sharma et al., 2015; Khanshour et al., 2018; Haller et al., 2016; Baschal et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2007; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Most AIS-associated genes showed the strongest expression levels in cartilage relative to other adolescent spinal tissues.
source: In all, most AIS-associated genes showed the strongest expression levels in cartilage relative to other adolescent spinal tissues.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In P0.5 mouse spines, strong collagen α1(XI) staining was observed in the nucleus pulposus and in surrounding annulus fibrosus.
source: In spines of P0.5 mice, strong staining was observed in the nucleus pulposus (NP) and in surrounding annulus fibrosus (AF) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In thoracic spines of P28 mice, strong collagen α1(XI) staining was observed in each compartment of the IVD.
source: In thoracic spines of P28 mice, the compartments of the IVD were more distinct, and strong collagen α1(XI) staining was observed in each (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In regions of the cartilage endplate-vertebral bone transition, collagen α1(XI) was detected in columnar chondrocytes, particularly in the hypertrophic zone adjacent to condensing bone.
source: In regions of the cartilage endplate (CEP)-vertebral bone transition, collagen α1(XI) was detected in columnar chondrocytes, particularly in the hypertrophic zone adjacent to condensing bone (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In P28 rib growth plates, a biphasic pattern of collagen α1(XI) reactivity was observed with most pronounced staining around cells of the presumed resting and pre-hypertrophic/hypertrophic zones.
source: In P28 rib growth plates, as in spine, a biphasic pattern was observed in which collagen α1(XI) reactivity was most pronounced around cells of the presumed resting and pre-hypertrophic/hypertrophic zones (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In mouse, collagen α1(XI) is detectable in all compartments of young postnatal IVD.
source: These data show that in mouse, collagen α1(XI) is detectable in all compartments of young postnatal IVD and, at the thoracic level, is particularly abundant in the chondro-osseous junction region of IVD and vertebral growth plate.
evidence: This is a summary of the immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: At the thoracic level, collagen α1(XI) is particularly abundant in the chondro-osseous junction region of IVD and vertebral growth plate in mouse.
source: These data show that in mouse, collagen α1(XI) is detectable in all compartments of young postnatal IVD and, at the thoracic level, is particularly abundant in the chondro-osseous junction region of IVD and vertebral growth plate.
evidence: This is a summary of the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Pax1 is a well-described marker of condensing sclerotomal cells as they form segments that will eventually become the IVD and vertebrae of the spine.
source: Pax1 is a well-described marker of condensing sclerotomal cells as they form segments that will eventually become the IVD and vertebrae of the spine (Chan et al., 2014; Aszódi et al., 1998; Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chan et al., 2014; Aszódi et al., 1998; Smith et al., 2011.

claim: Homozygous Pax1-/- mice were viable and developed spine deformity and kinks in the tail.
source: Homozygous Pax1-/- mice were viable and developed spine deformity and kinks in the tail, as observed in other Pax1-deficient mice (Wilm et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an observation from the Pax1 knockout mice generated in this study, consistent with prior reports.

claim: In wild-type IVD, strong overlapping expression of collagen α1(XI) and PAX1 cells was observed, mostly within the CEP and chondro-osseous interface.
source: In wild-type IVD, strong overlapping expression of collagen α1(XI) and PAX1 cells was observed, mostly within the CEP and chondro-osseous interface (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PAX1 staining was negative in Pax1-/- mice.
source: PAX1 staining was negative in Pax1-/- mice as expected, and collagen α1(XI) staining was dramatically diminished in CEP and the chondro-osseous vertebral borders.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Collagen α1(XI) staining was dramatically diminished in CEP and the chondro-osseous vertebral borders in Pax1-/- mice.
source: PAX1 staining was negative in Pax1-/- mice as expected, and collagen α1(XI) staining was dramatically diminished in CEP and the chondro-osseous vertebral borders.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The IVD in Pax1-/- mice was highly disorganized, without discernable NP, AF, and CEP structures.
source: Moreover, the IVD in Pax1-/- mice was highly disorganized, without discernable NP, AF, and CEP structures as has been reported (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Wallin et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and citation to Wallin et al., 1994.

claim: Gene-set enrichment analysis of RNAseq from E12.5 Pax1-/- versus wild-type tail tissue was most significant for the gene ontology term 'extracellular matrix'.
source: Gene-set enrichment analysis of RNAseq was most significant for the gene ontology term 'extracellular matrix' (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Expression of Col11a1 was significantly reduced in female and male Pax1-/- mice compared to wild-type mice.
source: By qRT-PCR analysis, expression of Col11a1, Adgrg6, and Sox6 was significantly reduced in female and male Pax1-/- mice compared to wild-type mice (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D-G.

claim: Expression of Adgrg6 was significantly reduced in female and male Pax1-/- mice compared to wild-type mice.
source: By qRT-PCR analysis, expression of Col11a1, Adgrg6, and Sox6 was significantly reduced in female and male Pax1-/- mice compared to wild-type mice (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D-G.

claim: Expression of Sox6 was significantly reduced in female and male Pax1-/- mice compared to wild-type mice.
source: By qRT-PCR analysis, expression of Col11a1, Adgrg6, and Sox6 was significantly reduced in female and male Pax1-/- mice compared to wild-type mice (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D-G.

claim: Loss of Pax1 leads to reduced expression of Col11a1 and the AIS-associated genes Adgrg6 and Sox6 in affected tissue of the developing tail.
source: These data show that loss of Pax1 leads to reduced expression of Col11a1 and the AIS-associated genes Adgrg6 and Sox6 in affected tissue of the developing tail.
evidence: This is a summary of the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D-G.

claim: COL11A1 has been linked with ECM remodeling and invasiveness in some cancers.
source: COL11A1 has been linked with ECM remodeling and invasiveness in some cancers (Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2014.

claim: In solid tumors, COL11A1 has been shown to alter ECM remodeling by enhancing MMP3 expression in response to TGFΒ1.
source: In solid tumors, COL11A1 has been shown to alter ECM remodeling by enhancing MMP3 expression in response to TGFΒ1 (Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2014.

claim: MMP3 encodes matrix metalloproteinase 3, also known as stromolysin, an enzyme implicated in matrix degradation and remodeling in connective tissues.
source: MMP3 encodes matrix metalloproteinase 3, also known as stromolysin, an enzyme implicated in matrix degradation and remodeling in connective tissues (Mudgett et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mudgett et al., 1998.

claim: MMP3 mRNA expression is strong in human spinal cartilage and bone, but minimal in spinal muscle.
source: We confirmed strong MMP3 mRNA expression, relative to COL11A1, in human spinal cartilage and bone, but minimal expression in spinal muscle (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mmp3 expression was significantly increased in cells where Col11a1 mRNA expression was downregulated by about 70% compared to untreated cells.
source: We found that Mmp3 expression was significantly increased in cells where Col11a1 mRNA expression was downregulated by about 70% compared to untreated cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Western blotting demonstrated an ~2- to 5-fold increase in pro-, secreted, and active forms of Mmp3 protein when collagen α1(XI) was reduced.
source: Furthermore, western blotting in these cells demonstrated an ~2- to 5-fold increase in pro-, secreted, and active forms of Mmp3 protein when collagen α1(XI) was reduced.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The proteolytic processing of precursor MMP3 into active forms did not appear to be affected by Col11a1 expression.
source: The proteolytic processing per se of precursor MMP3 into active forms (Sun et al., 2014) did not appear to be affected by Col11a1 expression (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an observation from western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mmp3 expression is negatively regulated by Col11a1 in mouse costal chondrocytes.
source: These results suggest that Mmp3 expression is negatively regulated by Col11a1 in mouse costal chondrocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the qRT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: ATC has been shown to harbor Cre-mediated recombination activity in most differentiated chondrocytes and in NP within 2 days of treating pregnant mothers with doxycycline starting at E15.5.
source: ATC has been shown to harbor Cre-mediated recombination activity in most differentiated chondrocytes and in NP within 2 days of treating pregnant mothers with doxycycline starting at E15.5 (Dy et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dy et al., 2012.

claim: Strong Cre activity was seen in P0 pups of mothers treated with doxycycline at E15.5 in the NP, CEP, and AF of the IVD and in chondrocytes of the growth plates.
source: Strong Cre activity was seen in P0 pups of mothers treated with doxycycline at E15.5 in the NP, CEP, and AF of the IVD and in chondrocytes of the growth plates (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cartilage from mice deficient in Col11a1 showed ~4-fold upregulation of Mmp3 mRNA expression relative to Col11a1fl/fl mice.
source: Consistent with results obtained by in vitro excision of Col11a1, cartilage from mice deficient in Col11a1 showed ~4-fold upregulation of Mmp3 mRNA expression relative to Col11a1fl/fl mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The AIS-associated variant P1335L occurs at the third position of a Gly-X-Y repeat in COL11A1.
source: Although low-resolution structures currently available for collagen triple helices are not useful for modeling the effects of individual variants on protein stability, we noted that the AIS-associated variant P1335L occurs at the third position of a Gly-X-Y repeat and consequently could be structurally important in promoting stability of the triple helix, particularly if it is hydroxylated.
evidence: This is an observation about the structural location of the variant.

claim: The P1335L variant could be structurally important in promoting stability of the collagen triple helix, particularly if it is hydroxylated.
source: Although low-resolution structures currently available for collagen triple helices are not useful for modeling the effects of individual variants on protein stability, we noted that the AIS-associated variant P1335L occurs at the third position of a Gly-X-Y repeat and consequently could be structurally important in promoting stability of the triple helix, particularly if it is hydroxylated.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural location of the variant.

claim: The P1335L variant is predicted to be deleterious by CADD and GERP analysis (CADD = 25.7; GERP = 5.75).
source: We also noted that this variant is predicted to be deleterious by Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion (CADD) (Rentzsch et al., 2021) and Genomic Evolutionary Rate Profiling (GERP) (Cooper et al., 2005) analysis (CADD = 25.7; GERP = 5.75).
evidence: This is supported by computational prediction tools CADD and GERP.

claim: COL11A1 missense variants have been shown to evoke transcriptional changes in ECM genes in cancer cells.
source: Further, COL11A1 missense variants have been shown to evoke transcriptional changes in ECM genes in cancer cells (Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2021.

claim: Overexpressing human wild-type COL11A1 suppressed Mmp3 expression in mouse chondrocytes.
source: Overexpressing human wild-type COL11A1 suppressed Mmp3 expression, consistent with the negative regulation we previously observed (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The COL11A1P1335L mutant failed to downregulate Mmp3 expression despite being overexpressed.
source: However, the COL11A1P1335L mutant failed to downregulate Mmp3 expression despite being overexpressed (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Regulation of Mmp3 appeared to be perturbed in the presence of the COL11A1P1335L variant in chondrocytes.
source: Thus, regulation of Mmp3 appeared to be perturbed in the presence of the COL11A1P1335L variant in these cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the qRT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The expression of Col11a1, and of other ECM genes, is known to be estrogen-responsive in certain tissues, such as ovarian follicular cells.
source: The expression of Col11a1, and of other ECM genes, is known to be estrogen- responsive in certain tissues, such as ovarian follicular cells (Zalewski et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zalewski et al., 2012.

claim: Mmp3 mRNA and protein levels were significantly increased after Col11a1 knockdown in wild-type chondrocytes.
source: We first validated that Mmp3 mRNA and protein levels were significantly increased after Col11a1 knockdown in wild-type chondrocytes, as observed by Cre-mediated deletion in Col11a1fl/fl chondrocytes (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Estrogen receptor 2 (Esr2), but not estrogen receptor alpha (Esr1), was detected in mouse chondrocytes by qRT-PCR.
source: Estrogen receptor 2 (Esr2), but not estrogen receptor alpha (Esr1), was detected in mouse chondrocytes by qRT-PCR (data not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from qRT-PCR experiments.

claim: After Esr2 knockdown, Col11a1 was significantly upregulated compared to scramble control.
source: After Esr2 knockdown, Col11a1 as well as Pax1 was significantly upregulated compared to scramble control, while Mmp3 expression was significantly downregulated (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: After Esr2 knockdown, Pax1 was significantly upregulated compared to scramble control.
source: After Esr2 knockdown, Col11a1 as well as Pax1 was significantly upregulated compared to scramble control, while Mmp3 expression was significantly downregulated (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: After Esr2 knockdown, Mmp3 expression was significantly downregulated compared to scramble control.
source: After Esr2 knockdown, Col11a1 as well as Pax1 was significantly upregulated compared to scramble control, while Mmp3 expression was significantly downregulated (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Col11a1 knockdown upregulated Pax1 expression, suggesting a negative feedback loop between Pax1 and Col11a1 in chondrocytes.
source: We also performed Col11a1 knockdowns in these cells and noted upregulation of Pax1 expression, suggesting a negative feedback loop between Pax1 and Col11a1 in these cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an inference based on qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Simultaneous knockdown of Col11a1 and Esr2 expression reduced Mmp3 expression to normal levels.
source: Simultaneous knockdown of Col11a1 and Esr2 expression reduced Mmp3 expression to normal levels, supporting a possible interaction between Col11a1 and Esr2 in regulating Mmp3.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Treating chondrocytes with tamoxifen upregulated Col11a1 expression to similar levels as observed after Esr2 knockdown, compared to cells treated with DMSO carrier.
source: Treating chondrocytes with tamoxifen, an estrogen receptor modulator, also upregulated Col11a1 expression to similar levels as observed after Esr2 knockdown, compared to cells treated with DMSO carrier (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Estrogen signaling suppresses Col11a1 expression in chondrocytes.
source: These results suggest that estrogen signaling suppresses Col11a1 expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Esr2 knockdown and tamoxifen treatment data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In cultured rat CEP cells, Esr2 mRNA was downregulated after Col11a1 knockdown.
source: In cultured rat CEP cells, Esr2 mRNA was downregulated, and Mmp3 mRNA was upregulated after Col11a1 knockdown, as observed in mouse chondrocytes (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In cultured rat CEP cells, Mmp3 mRNA was upregulated after Col11a1 knockdown.
source: In cultured rat CEP cells, Esr2 mRNA was downregulated, and Mmp3 mRNA was upregulated after Col11a1 knockdown, as observed in mouse chondrocytes (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Esr2 knockdown did not significantly impact Col11a1 or Mmp3 expression in rat CEP cells.
source: However, Esr2 knockdown did not significantly impact Col11a1 or Mmp3 expression in these cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In cultured mouse chondrocytes, ESR2 signaling disrupts the suppression of Mmp3 by Col11a1.
source: Hence, we conclude that in cultured mouse chondrocytes, ESR2 signaling disrupts the suppression of Mmp3 by Col11a1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Collagen type XI is composed of three chains encoded by the COL11A1, COL11A2, and COL2A1 genes.
source: The results of this study together with the previous observation of COL11A2 rare variant enrichment in AIS support a role for the collagen α1(XI) heterotrimer itself in its pathogenesis (Haller et al., 2016). Collagen type XI, composed of three chains encoded by the COL11A1, COL11A2, and COL2A1 genes (OMIM #s 120280,120290, 120140, respectively), is a minor component of collagen type II fibrils that are abundant in cartilage.
evidence: This is established knowledge about collagen type XI composition.

claim: Collagen type XI is a minor component of collagen type II fibrils that are abundant in cartilage.
source: Collagen type XI, composed of three chains encoded by the COL11A1, COL11A2, and COL2A1 genes (OMIM #s 120280,120290, 120140, respectively), is a minor component of collagen type II fibrils that are abundant in cartilage.
evidence: This is established knowledge about collagen type XI function.

claim: Collagen type XI is broadly expressed in testis, trachea, tendons, trabecular bone, skeletal muscle, placenta, lung, brain neuroepithelium, the vitreous of the eye, and IVDs.
source: Collagen type XI is also broadly expressed in testis, trachea, tendons, trabecular bone, skeletal muscle, placenta, lung, brain neuroepithelium, the vitreous of the eye, and IVDs (Yoshioka et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yoshioka et al., 1995.

claim: In the pericellular space, collagen α1(XI) initiates fibrillogenesis with collagen type II fibrils, maintaining regular spacing and diameter of the collagen fibrils.
source: In the pericellular space, collagen α1(XI) initiates fibrillogenesis with collagen type II fibrils, maintaining regular spacing and diameter of the collagen fibrils, while organizing the pericellular surface by interaction with cartilage proteoglycans (Smith et al., 1989; Luo and Karsdal, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Smith et al., 1989 and Luo and Karsdal, 2019.

claim: Collagen α1(XI) organizes the pericellular surface by interaction with cartilage proteoglycans.
source: In the pericellular space, collagen α1(XI) initiates fibrillogenesis with collagen type II fibrils, maintaining regular spacing and diameter of the collagen fibrils, while organizing the pericellular surface by interaction with cartilage proteoglycans (Smith et al., 1989; Luo and Karsdal, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Smith et al., 1989 and Luo and Karsdal, 2019.

claim: Purified human collagen type XI, when added back to chondrocytes in in vitro culture, stimulates chondrogenesis while inhibiting hypertrophy.
source: Purified human collagen type XI, when added back to chondrocytes in in vitro culture, stimulates chondrogenesis while inhibiting hypertrophy, as measured by histological staining, proliferation assays, and relative expression of chondrogenic early marker genes (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2018.

claim: In newborn and 1-month-old mice, collagen α1(XI) was abundant in IVD and at the chondro-osseous junction of IVD and vertebrae, particularly concentrated in pre-hypertrophic/hypertrophic chondrocytic cells.
source: In newborn and 1-month-old mice, we found that collagen α1(XI) was abundant in IVD and at the chondro-osseous junction of IVD and vertebrae, particularly concentrated in pre-hypertrophic/hypertrophic chondrocytic cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: At E16.5, Col11a1 expression was highest in cells with signatures of pre-hypertrophic to hypertrophic transition, and lowest in cells with osteogenic signatures in long bone growth plates.
source: In long bone growth plates, Long et al., 2022, recently identified eight distinct cell clusters after unsupervised analysis of single cell (scRNAseq) of flow-sorted hypertrophic chondrocytes from Col10a1Cre;Rosa26fs-tdTomato mice. At E16.5, Col11a1 expression was highest in cells with signatures of pre-hypertrophic to hypertrophic transition, and lowest in cells with osteogenic signatures (M Hilton, personal communication) (Long et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Long et al., 2022 and personal communication.

claim: Collagen α1(XI) normally participates in maintaining growth plate cells in a hypertrophic, pre-osteogenic state.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that collagen α1(XI) normally participates in maintaining growth plate cells in a hypertrophic, pre-osteogenic state, although little is known about its precise molecular function in that compartment, or in the IVD, during spinal development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern and functional data cited.

claim: Spines of Col11a1-deficient mice (cho/cho) show incompletely formed vertebral bodies, spinal curvatures, and decreased separation between vertebrae.
source: Spines of Col11a1-deficient mice (cho/cho) show incompletely formed vertebral bodies, spinal curvatures, and decreased separation between vertebrae, which are themselves less mineralized than in wild-type mice (Hafez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hafez et al., 2015.

claim: Vertebrae in Col11a1-deficient mice (cho/cho) are less mineralized than in wild-type mice.
source: Spines of Col11a1-deficient mice (cho/cho) show incompletely formed vertebral bodies, spinal curvatures, and decreased separation between vertebrae, which are themselves less mineralized than in wild-type mice (Hafez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hafez et al., 2015.

claim: Common COL11A1 variants have been associated with adult lumbar disc herniation and lumbar disc degeneration.
source: Notably, common COL11A1 variants also have been associated with adult lumbar disc herniation and lumbar disc degeneration, as well as DXA-measured bone size, spinal stenosis, and spondylolisthesis (Jiang et al., 2017; Mio et al., 2007; Styrkarsdottir et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jiang et al., 2017; Mio et al., 2007; Styrkarsdottir et al., 2019.

claim: Common COL11A1 variants have been associated with DXA-measured bone size, spinal stenosis, and spondylolisthesis.
source: Notably, common COL11A1 variants also have been associated with adult lumbar disc herniation and lumbar disc degeneration, as well as DXA-measured bone size, spinal stenosis, and spondylolisthesis (Jiang et al., 2017; Mio et al., 2007; Styrkarsdottir et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jiang et al., 2017; Mio et al., 2007; Styrkarsdottir et al., 2019.

claim: Reduction in the components of collagen type XI disrupts spinal development.
source: Although gain-of-function or dominant-negative effects of the rs3753841 variant would not have been revealed in our assays, the spinal deformity noted in the cho/cho loss-of-function model, and failure of missense variants in Col11a2 to rescue congenital scoliosis (Rebello et al., 2023), leads us to surmise that reduction in the components of collagen type XI disrupts spinal development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cho/cho mouse model and the zebrafish rescue experiments.

claim: Pax1 activates a gene expression cascade starting at E12.5–13.5 in mouse development.
source: Pax1 is a well-described marker of early spine development, where it activates a gene expression cascade starting at E12.5–13.5 in mouse development (Wilm et al., 1998; Rodrigo et al., 2003; Sivakamasundari et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wilm et al., 1998; Rodrigo et al., 2003; Sivakamasundari et al., 2017.

claim: The downregulation of Col11a1 in Pax1-/- mice is consistent with a prior study of gene expression in flow-sorted GFP-labeled Pax1-/- embryonic IVD cells.
source: The downregulation of Col11a1 is consistent with a prior study of gene expression in flow-sorted GFP-labeled Pax1-/- embryonic IVD cells (Sivakamasundari et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sivakamasundari et al., 2017.

claim: Col11a1 expression in developing tail is likely directly activated by binding SOX transcription factors.
source: It is likely, however, that Col11a1 expression in developing tail is directly activated by binding SOX transcription factors, as a prior genomic study using chromatin immunoprecipitation and sequencing in rat chondrosarcoma cells identified super enhancers near the Col11a1 gene that were bound multiple times by SOX9 and SOX6 (Liu and Lefebvre, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on citation to Liu and Lefebvre, 2015.

claim: The SOX5/6/9 trio is known to regulate many of the same genes as PAX1.
source: The SOX5/6/9 trio is known to regulate many of the same genes as PAX1 (Sivakamasundari et al., 2017), but whether this includes Col11a1 is unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sivakamasundari et al., 2017.

claim: The endplate is important as the site allowing diffusion of nutrients from the circulation into the avascular inner IVD.
source: The endplate, which is important as the site allowing diffusion of nutrients from the circulation into the avascular inner IVD, harbors subpopulations of cells expressing type II collagen presumably organized by collagen type XI (Chan et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chan et al., 2014 and Smith et al., 2011.

claim: The endplate harbors subpopulations of cells expressing type II collagen presumably organized by collagen type XI.
source: The endplate, which is important as the site allowing diffusion of nutrients from the circulation into the avascular inner IVD, harbors subpopulations of cells expressing type II collagen presumably organized by collagen type XI (Chan et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chan et al., 2014 and Smith et al., 2011.

claim: In humans the endplate and vertebrae become distinctly separate structures with closure of the growth plates at puberty.
source: While the endplate is continuous with the vertebral growth plate in mice, it is important to note that in humans the endplate and vertebrae become distinctly separate structures with closure of the growth plates at puberty (Chan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chan et al., 2014.

claim: Lagging maturity of the ring apophysis, combined with mechanical forces across the IVD in the horizontal plane, has been proposed as an initiating factor leading to rotatory decompensation in the adolescent spine in AIS.
source: Lagging maturity of the ring apophysis, combined with mechanical forces across the IVD in the horizontal plane, has been proposed as an initiating factor leading to rotatory decompensation in the adolescent spine in AIS (Costa et al., 2021; Castelein et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Costa et al., 2021 and Castelein et al., 2020.

claim: Sun et al. reported the discovery of a vertebral skeletal stem cell (vSSC) residing in the endplate and marked by expression of the genes Zic1 and Pax1.
source: Recently, Sun et al. reported the discovery of a vertebral skeletal stem cell (vSSC) residing in the endplate and marked by expression of the genes Zic1 and Pax1, along with other cell surface markers (Sun et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2023.

claim: Vertebral skeletal stem cells (vSSCs) express high levels of Col11a1.
source: These vSSCs also express high levels of Col11a1 (M Greenblatt, personal communication).
evidence: This is supported by personal communication.

claim: AIS-associated variation in collagen α1(XI), perhaps together with mechanical forces, could alter the differentiation trajectory of the vertebral skeletal stem cell niche.
source: It is interesting to consider that AIS-associated variation in collagenα1(XI), perhaps together with mechanical forces, could alter the differentiation trajectory of this cell niche.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings about vSSCs and Col11a1 expression.

claim: Cell populations at the IVD-vertebral junction region are relevant in AIS pathogenesis.
source: Altogether, extant data and our results strongly suggest that cell populations at the IVD-vertebral junction region are relevant in AIS pathogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization and expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Matrix metalloproteinase 3 is a secreted enzyme expressed in connective tissues and in regions of endochondral ossification.
source: Matrix metalloproteinase 3, also known as stromolysin, is a secreted enzyme expressed in connective tissues and in regions of endochondral ossification (Ortega et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ortega et al., 2004.

claim: MMP3 has degradative activity toward a variety of ECM components, including proteoglycans, fibronectin, laminin, but notably not type I collagen.
source: MMP3 has degradative activity toward a variety of ECM components, including proteoglycans, fibronectin, laminin, but notably not type I collagen (Sellers and Murphy, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sellers and Murphy, 1981.

claim: In chondrocytes MMP3 has been shown to translocate to the nucleus, where it activates transcription of connective tissue growth factor (CTGF/CCN2) by binding to an element known as transcription enhancer dominant in chondrocytes (TRENDIC).
source: Additionally, in chondrocytes MMP3 also has been shown to translocate to the nucleus, where it activates transcription of connective tissue growth factor (CTGF/CCN2) by binding to an element known as transcription enhancer dominant in chondrocytes (TRENDIC) (Eguchi et al., 2008; Cui et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eguchi et al., 2008 and Cui et al., 2017.

claim: Col11a1 variation may have consequences for both MMP3 enzymatic activity levels and MMP3-mediated transcriptional programming in chondrocytes and CEP cells.
source: Our observations of a Col11a1-Mmp3 signaling axis in chondrocytes and CEP cells raise the possibility that Col11a1 variation may have consequences for both MMP3 enzymatic activity levels and MMP3-mediated transcriptional programming in these cells.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings about Col11a1-Mmp3 regulation.

claim: COL11A1 missense variants, usually altering glycine or proline in Gly-X-Y repeats in the collagen α1(XI) helical domain, are reported to be frequent in cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas.
source: COL11A1 missense variants, usually altering glycine or proline in Gly-X-Y repeats in the collagen α1(XI) helical domain as with COL11A1P1335L, are reported to be frequent in cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas and have been linked to transcriptional changes and tumor invasiveness (Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2021.

claim: COL11A1 missense variants have been linked to transcriptional changes and tumor invasiveness.
source: COL11A1 missense variants, usually altering glycine or proline in Gly-X-Y repeats in the collagen α1(XI) helical domain as with COL11A1P1335L, are reported to be frequent in cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas and have been linked to transcriptional changes and tumor invasiveness (Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2021.

claim: The mechanisms by which chondrocytes or other cells sense single amino acid changes in collagen α1(XI) and induce subsequent transcriptional responses are unknown but may involve direct interaction with integrins in the pericellular space.
source: The mechanisms by which chondrocytes or other cells sense such single amino acid changes in collagen α1(XI) and induce subsequent transcriptional responses are unknown but may involve direct interaction with integrins in the pericellular space (Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to Lee et al., 2021.

claim: Type XI collagen is a key player in organizing the pericellular space, which is critical for transmitting mechanical forces from the ECM to the cell.
source: We found that Col11a1 expression is sensitive to estrogen receptor blockade or knockdown in chondrocytes. Type XI collagen is also a key player in organizing the pericellular space, which is critical for transmitting mechanical forces from the ECM to the cell (Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2016.

claim: Type XI collagen may effectively act as a receptor for environmental cues, i.e., mechanical forces and estrogen signaling, in the adolescent spine.
source: Thus, it is interesting to consider that type XI collagen may effectively act as a receptor for environmental cues, i.e., mechanical forces and estrogen signaling, in the adolescent spine.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings about Col11a1 expression and regulation.
